clips.title: You Need a Private Claude Plugin Marketplace (Cowork)
clips.why: He starts from the same problem as our Monday: skills scattered across people and copied by hand, and then explains what a private marketplace is.
look: The scattered skills problem: copies that drift apart, which is why one shared repository matters.
Why he says it matters for agents as well as people: an agent needs the same tools as the team.
What a marketplace really is: a repository with a catalog that lists plugins.
clips.after: Our marketplace is one private repository too, read by every engineer and by Nova; this lesson adds the part he does not cover: which commit each machine reads.

clips.title: Google Chrome "Release Channels" - Which to Choose?
clips.why: Chrome's Stable and Beta channels are the classic example of one product released at two speeds, which is exactly what our stable and main branches do for skills.
look: Stable is what almost everyone should run, because changes reach it only after they were tried elsewhere.
Beta gets changes earlier and accepts that some will break; those users find the problems for everyone else.
The channels are the same product, only the timing differs.
clips.after: Our pilots are the Beta users: they read main and meet a broken skill first, so stable, which every engineer and agent reads, only receives what survived a week.

practice.q: Add our marketplace so that you only get what was promoted to the stable branch.
practice.hint: The name of the branch everyone reads.
practice.why: The part after # is the ref. Without it, Claude Code reads the default branch, main, and every merge reaches you.

practice.q: Put the life of one skill change in order.
items: A pull request changes the verify skill and raises rhino-core's version
It is merged into main, and pilots on the latest channel get it at their next refresh
The nightly evals stay green for a week and no pilot reports a problem
Someone fast-forwards stable to main's commit
Every other laptop and every new agent machine refreshes and replaces its cached copy
practice.why: main is where a change is tried, stable is where it is trusted, and the version bump is what makes each laptop replace its copy.

practice.q: Why do we promote by fast-forwarding stable to main, instead of cherry-picking the good commits onto stable?

options.text: So stable holds exactly the commits the pilots ran for a week, and nothing they never tested
options.why: A cherry-picked stable is a new combination of changes that nobody ran together.

options.text: Because git cannot cherry-pick between branches of one repository
options.why: It can. The reason is about what was tested, not what git allows.

options.text: Because a fast-forward raises the plugin's version automatically
options.why: Nothing raises the version for you. The pull request that changed the plugin did, and CI checks it.

practice.q: Where should a plugin's version be written in our repository?

options.text: In the catalog entry in marketplace.json, so people see it when they browse
options.why: If plugin.json also has a version, it wins without a word, and the two can drift. validate warns about exactly that.

options.text: In both, kept equal by hand
options.why: Two copies of one number drift sooner or later, and the catalog copy is ignored anyway.

options.text: Only in the plugin's own plugin.json
options.why: That is the value Claude Code reads first. One place means one truth, and our CI checks that it rises with every change.
